books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Secession dates verified against the Ordinance of Secession table (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinance_of_Secession), the American Battlefield Trust Civil War timeline (battlefields.org), and Digital History, University of Houston (digitalhistory.uh.edu). Texas adopted its ordinance February 1, 1861, confirmed by popular referendum February 23; Virginia's ordinance was ratified by referendum May 23, 1861.
stimulus.text:
Ordinances of secession, in the order the states adopted them. Seven states seceded before Lincoln's inauguration on March 4, 1861; four more followed after the firing on Fort Sumter.

| State | Date of ordinance |
| South Carolina | December 20, 1860 |
| Mississippi | January 9, 1861 |
| Florida | January 10, 1861 |
| Alabama | January 11, 1861 |
| Georgia | January 19, 1861 |
| Louisiana | January 26, 1861 |
| Texas | February 1, 1861 |
| Virginia | April 17, 1861 |
| Arkansas | May 6, 1861 |
| Tennessee | May 6, 1861 |
| North Carolina | May 20, 1861 |

Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri were slave states that stayed in the Union and are not listed.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The pattern in the table best supports which conclusion?

options.text: Secession came in two waves: Deep South first, Upper South later.
All eleven states seceded in the same week in 1861.
options.misconception: The dates run from December 1860 to May 1861, five months, not one week.

options.text: The border states seceded last, after North Carolina.
options.misconception: The border states never seceded; the table says they stayed in the Union.

options.text: Texas seceded before South Carolina in December 1860.
options.misconception: Texas adopted its ordinance February 1, 1861, six weeks after South Carolina.

rationales.A: Seven states cluster between December 20 and February 1, then nothing until April 17, when four more follow. Background: the gap is the Fort Sumter crisis — the second wave answered Lincoln's call for troops.
rationales.B: The dates run from December 1860 to May 1861, five months, not one week.
rationales.C: The border states never seceded; the table says they stayed in the Union.
rationales.D: Texas adopted its ordinance February 1, 1861, six weeks after South Carolina.
rationales.general:
1. Group the dates: seven before March, four after April.
2. The gap between February 1 and April 17 is the pause.
3. Background: the Upper South waited through the winter, hoping for compromise, until Sumter and the troop call forced a choice.
4. A table with a gap in the middle is telling you about the gap.
Remember: cluster the dates before you read them one by one — the clusters are the argument.
